div.p: Objective This study aimed to evaluate CTF1 expression in glioma, its relationship to patient prognosis and the tumor immune microenvironment, and effects on glioma phenotypes to identify a new therapeutic target for treating glioma precisely.

div.head: Methods
div.p: We initially assessed the expression of CTF1, a member of the IL-6 family, in glioma, using bioinformatics tools and publicly available databases. Furthermore, we examined the correlation between CTF1 expression and tumor prognosis, DNA methylation patterns, m6A-related genes, potential biological functions, the immune microenvironment, and genes associated with immune checkpoints. We also explored potential associations with drug sensitivity. To assess the impact on glioma cell proliferation and apoptosis, we employed various assays, including the Cell Counting Kit-8, colony formation assay, and flow cytometry.

Results CTF1 gene and protein expression were significantly elevated in glioma tissues, and correlated with malignancy and poor prognosis. CTF1 was an independent prognostic factor and negatively associated with DNA methylation. The involvement of CTF1 in m6A modifications contributed to glioma progression. Enrichment analysis revealed immune response pathways linked with CTF1 in glioma, including natural killer cell cytotoxicity, NOD-like receptor signaling, Toll-like receptor signaling, antigen processing, chemokine signaling, and cytokine receptor interactions. CTF1 expression correlated positively with pathways related to apoptosis, inflammation, proliferation, and epithelial-mesenchymal transition, and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling. Additionally, CTF1 expression was positively associated with macrophage, eosinophil, and neutrophil contents and immune checkpoint-related genes, but negatively associated with sensitivity to 14 drugs. In vitro experiments confirmed that CTF1 knockdown inhibited glioma cell proliferation and promoted apoptosis.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Glioma is the predominant primary malignant brain tumor in the central nervous system, representing 80%-85% of such tumors in adults [1]. Gliomas are classified into four grades (1)(2)(3)(4) according to the fifth edition of the World Health Organization (WHO) Classification of Central Nervous System Tumors [2]. Generally, WHO classifies grade 2 and 3 gliomas as lower grade gliomas (LGG), while grade 4 gliomas are known as glioblastomas (GBM). Currently, optimal tumor surgical resection, adjuvant radiotherapy, and chemotherapy using the alkylating agent temozolomide remain the primary treatment modalities for glioma, particularly glioblastoma. Nevertheless, due to the unique location of intracranial glioma, its highly invasive growth characteristics, resistant to traditional radiochemotherapy, and associated side effects, the patients with malignant glioma remain susceptible to relapse post-surgery despite the implementation of standard and precision treatments, resulting in poor prognosis.

e CTF1 protein, encoded by the cardiotrophin 1 (CTF1/CT-1) gene, belongs to the interleukin-6 (IL-6) family of cytokines. e IL-6, IL-11, IL-27, IL-31, oncostatin M (OSM), leukemia inhibitory factor (LIF), ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF), and cardiotrophin-like cytokine factor 1(CLCF1) genes are all part of this family [3]. CTF1 demonstrates pleiotropic functions across several tissues and cell types. Initially, it was predominantly associated with the cardiovascular system, where it has been shown to be closely linked to the onset and progression of various cardiovascular diseases [4][5][6][7]. Subsequent studies have revealed its protective effects in other organs, including the liver, kidney and bone [8][9][10]. Furthermore, emerging studies indicate that CTF1 may play a significant role in the pathophysiology of various metabolic disorders [11,12], but, its role in cancer is less well documented [13,14], with only a few studies linking it to tumor development and progression. For instance, tumor-derived CTF1 has been recognized as a crucial regulator of matrix-assisted migration, invasion, and metastasis in breast cancer cells, through mechanisms that depend on autophagy [15]. Additionally, patients with uveal melanoma with elevated levels of CTF1 expression have a worse prognosis [16]. In lung adenocarcinoma, CTF1 expression is reduced and negatively correlates with prognosis [17]. However, the expression and biological function of CTF1 in gliomas have not been investigated.

In recent years, bioinformatics approaches have been extensively used to discover molecular markers associated with tumors. Our study examined the expression of CTF1 in patients with glioma and its correlation with prognosis using multiple publicly available datasets and online bioinformatics analysis platforms. Additionally, we explored the potential biological role of CTF1 and its interaction with various immune cell infiltrates within the tumor immune microenvironment.

div.head: Cell culture
div.p: Our laboratory provided the glioma cell lines U118MG and LN229. Cell lines were incubated in a humidified incubator at 37 °C with 5% CO 2 . Cells were cultured in high-glucose DMEM medium (VivaCell BIOSCEINCES, C3113-0500) containing 12% fetal bovine serum (NEWZERUM, FBS-S500).

div.head: Cell transfection
div.p: During logarithmic growth, cells were seeded into 6-well plates and transfected with siRNA when they reached 40% confluence. Solutions A (serum-free DMEM with si-CTF1) and B [serum-free DMEM with Lipofectamine 2000 (Invitrogen, 11668-019)] were prepared, incubated separately, combined, and added to each well. After a 6-h incubation, the medium was replaced with complete culture medium for cell proliferation and colony formation studies. Cells were harvested after 48 h of cultivation for additional experiments. e siRNA sequences for CTF1 knockdown are in Table 1.

div.head: Reverse transcription quantitative real-time PCR (RT-qPCR)
div.p: RT-qPCR was performed using the TB Green ® Premix Ex TaqTM Kit (Takara, RR420Q) and the ABI QuantStudio 5, with the GAPDH gene mRNA expression level used as the internal reference. e cDNA generated from reverse transcription of the total RNA sample was used as the template for analysis.
e primer sequences are listed in Table 2. e primers were synthesized by Beijing Tianyi Huiyuan Biotechnology Co., Ltd.

div.head: Cell counting Kit-8 (CCK8)
div.p: Cells were collected, quantified, and cultured at a density of 1000 cells per well in a 96-well plate, including control wells. CCK-8 (DOJINDO Chemical Technology, CK04) diluent mixed with DMEM was added, and the absorbance at 450 nm was measured after 1 h of incubation at 37 °C using an enzyme-labeler. Daily absorbance readings from Day 0 to Day 5 were collected and used to create the cell growth curve.

div.head: Colony formation experiment
div.p: Cells were counted, seeded into 6-well plates (2000 cells per well for U118MG and 1000 cells per well for LN229), and incubated at 37 °C in 5% CO 2 for approximately 10 days. Visible colonies were fixed in methanol (Beijing Beihua Kaiyuan Chemical Co., Ltd, 20230207) for 30 min, stained with 0.1% crystal violet (Changsha Dingguo Biotechnology Co., Ltd, 548-62-9) solution, and then rinsed with distilled water. After drying, the colonies were photographed and counted.

div.head: Cell apoptosis
div.p: To detect cell apoptosis, we used the Annexin V FITC Apoptosis Detection Kit (DOJINDO Chemical Technology, AD10). After 48 h of cell knockdown in a 6-well plate, the cell culture supernatant was transferred to a 5-mL centrifuge tube. Cells were then washed with phosphate buffered saline (PBS, Gibco, 10010023), and the wash solution was collected. Subsequently, the cells were digested with 0.4 mL trypsin (Gibco, 15090046) and the digestion was terminated by adding 0.8 mL of complete culture medium. e cell suspension was centrifuged at 1,000 rpm for 3 min, resuspended in PBS, and centrifuged again. An appropriate volume of pre-prepared 1× Annexin V Binding Solution was added for a final cell concentration of 3 to 5×10 6 cells/mL. Next, 100 μL of the cell suspension was placed in a flow cytometry tube. 5 μL of Annexin V FITC conjugate and 5 μL of PI solution were added, and the mixture incubated in the dark for 15 min at room temperature. Subsequently, 400 μL of 1× Annexin V binding solution was added, the sample was kept on ice, and it was analyzed by flow cytometry within 1 h.

div.head: Data sourcing
div.p: Glioma RNA-seq data and associated clinical details were sourced from e Cancer Genome Atlas Program (TCGA) via their official portal (https:// portal. gdc. cancer. gov) and the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project (https:// commo nfund. nih. gov). Both the TCGA and GTEx datasets were utilized in the pan-cancer analysis. Additionally, the GSE108474 dataset was sourced from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database (http:// www. ncbi. nlm. nih. gov/ geo/).

div.head: The expression of CTF1 in glioma samples versus normal samples
div.p: e TCGA and GTEx gene expression data were converted to Transcripts Per Million (TPM) format and processed using a logarithmic transformation. e rank sum test was used to examine differences in CTF1 expression across cancer types, with a focus on gliomas. e Cancer Proteogenomic Data Analysis Site (CPTAC) was used to compare the levels of CTF1 protein in glioma and normal brain tissue.

div.head: Examining the relationship between CTF1 expression and the characteristics of glioma patients
div.p: Based on the median expression level of CTF1, RNAseq data from glioma patients in the TCGA database were divided into two groups: 'high expression' and 'low expression' . is categorization aimed to explore whether the expression levels of CTF1 are correlated with the clinicopathological characteristics of glioma patients.

div.head: Examining the predictive significance of CTF1 in glioma patients
div.p: Glioma patient RNA-seq data from TCGA were grouped based on CTF1 median expression levels. Prognostic implications were evaluated using Kaplan-Meier survival plots and Log-rank tests to investigate their impacts on overall survival (OS), disease-specific survival (DSS), and the progression-free interval (PFI). Associations with patient outcomes across diverse clinical categories were examined. Additionally, CGGA and Rembrandt datasets were analyzed via GlioVis to confirm CTF1 expression's relationship with OS. Furthermore, we performed both univariate and multivariate Cox regression analyses to evaluate the correlation between CTF1 expression, clinicopathological factors, and patient outcomes in the glioma dataset sourced from TCGA. A forecast model was created and evaluated for accuracy using a calibration curve based on important data from the multivariate Cox regression analysis.

div.head: Analyzing DNA methylation in CTF1
div.p: e Shiny Methylation Analysis Resource Tool (SMART, http:// www. bioin fo-zs. com/ smart app) is a user-friendly website that utilizes TCGA data for DNA methylation correlation analysis. We employed this tool to visualize CpG sites related to CTF1 on the chromosomes.

div.head: Association between CTF1 expression and m6A-related genes
div.p: Based on the TCGA glioma dataset, the 'ggplot2' R package was utilized to analyze the relationship between CTF1 expression and m6A-related genes.

div.head: Analysis of the differences in single gene expression of CTF1 and the enrichment of differential gene functions
div.p: TCGA RNA-seq data from glioma patients were divided into two groups based on CTF1 median expression levels. Differentially expressed genes were identified using the 'DESeq2' R package, with selection criteria of |Log2FC|> 2 and an adjusted P-value (padj) < 0.05. A volcano plot displayed the differentially expressed genes, while a heatmap highlighted the top 10 upregulated genes. Afterwards, the first 100 upregulated genes were analyzed using Gene Ontology (GO) and the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) to explore their functional annotations and potential roles in biological pathways. Moreover, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) was performed on all CTF1-related differential genes to provide a better understanding of their functions. We used the 'GSVA' R package with the 'ssgsea' method to analyze the correlation between CTF1 expression and five cancer-related pathways using Spearman correlation analysis.

div.head: Examining the relationship between CTF1 and the tumor immune microenvironment
div.p: Utilizing the 'ESTIMATE' R package, we analyzed Stromal, Immune, and ESTIMATE scores in TCGA's glioma, GBM, and LGG datasets. We deployed the ssGSEA algorithm from the 'GSVA' R package to evaluate the correlation between CTF1 expression and immune infiltration. Meanwhile, we compared immune infiltration levels between groups with high and low CTF1 expression, using the median as a threshold. Furthermore, the expression levels of genes associated with immune checkpoints were analyzed and compared between groups exhibiting high and low expression of CTF1. Spearman's analysis assessed relationships between CTF1 expression and key immune checkpoints. Finally, the TISCH database (http:// tisch. comp-genom ics. org/) provided multiple datasets examining CTF1 expression patterns within the tumor microenvironment of various cell types.

div.head: Analyzing drug sensitivity of CTF1
div.p: Download NCI-60 compound activity data and RNAseq expression profiles from CellMiner ™ (https:// disco ver. nci. nih. gov/ CellM iner/ home. do) to study the link between CTF1 expression and drug sensitivity, focusing on FDA-approved or clinically tested drugs.

div.head: Statistical analysis
div.p: We used GraphPad Prism 9.0 for data analysis, applying one-way ANOVA or Student's t-tests as needed. Bioinformatics analyses involved the Wilcoxon rank sum test, Kruskal-Wallis test, Bonferroni-Dunn test, and Spearman test. R software (version 4.2.2) and online tools were used for statistical evaluations and data visualization. Significance was set at P < 0.05.

div.head: High levels of CTF1 in glioma are associated with a worse prognosis
div.p: In our study, we used the merged TCGA and GTEx databases to determine CTF1 expression in diverse cancers and revealed increased expression in GBM, LGG, and six other tumor types. In contrast, CTF1 levels were lower in adrenocortical carcinoma, colon adenocarcinoma, and 14 other tumors (Fig. 1A). Increased CTF1 expression in gliomas correlated with higher tumor grades (Fig. 1B). Both the GES108474 and CPTAC databases confirmed elevated CTF1 mRNA and protein expression in gliomas compared to those in normal tissues (Fig. 1C, D). TCGA data analysis identified a significant association between CTF1 overexpression and adverse clinicopathological features (Supplementary Fig. 1A-H). Kaplan-Meier survival analyses revealed worse outcomes for patients with high CTF1-expressing glioma, indicating its prognostic relevance (Fig. 1E-G). Confirmation using CGGA and Rembrandt datasets reinforced this finding (Supplementary Fig. 2A, B). Subgroup analysis revealed an inverse relationship between high CTF1 expression and OS, except for the 1p/19q codeletion subgroup (Supplementary Fig. 2C-Q). Cox regression analyses identified CTF1 expression alongside WHO grade, isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) status, age, and 1p/19q codeletion as crucial independent factors affecting glioma survival (Fig. 2A, B). A prognostic model incorporating these factors was developed (Fig. 2C), with calibration curves assessing its predictive accuracy for 1-, 3-, and 5-year OS probabilities in patients with glioma (Fig. 2D). Overall, our analyses suggest that elevated CTF1 expression is associated with adverse prognostic outcomes in patients with glioma.

div.head: Correlation of CTF1 expression with DNA methylation and m6A RNA modification in glioma
div.p: Our assessment of DNA methylation patterns revealed a consistent inverse correlation between CTF1 expression and methylation levels in the GBM and LGG subtypes. We identified nine GBM and eight LGG probes that featured concurrent reduced methylation level and heightened CTF1 expression, indicating a potential mechanism for CTF1 modification (Fig. 3A, B). Spatial analysis indicated distinct methylation profiles within CTF1-related probes, with highly methylated probes found on islands and S_Shore regions, signifying a specific genomic context for CTF1 regulation (Fig. 3C, D). Concurrently, we explored the interplay between CTF1 expression and m6A RNA modification and revealed significant correlations with various m6A-related genes (Fig. 3E). Stratification based on CTF1 levels revealed distinct expression patterns of m6A regulators, indicating their potential involvement in glioma development and prognosis, with particular emphasis on WTAP, IGF2BP2, and IGF2BP3 (Fig. 3F-H). Overall, our findings elucidate a potential association among CTF1 expression, DNA methylation, and m6A modifications, providing novel insights into glioma progression and prognosis.

div.head: Functional enrichment of CTF1
div.p: By investigating the TCGA glioma dataset, we identified 1436 differentially expressed genes between the high and low CTF1 expression groups. Among these, the expression levels of 1370 genes were upregulated, whereas 66 genes demonstrated downregulated expression (Fig. 4A). Visual representations via heatmaps showcased the top 10 differently expressed genes in both the high and low CTF1 expression groups (Fig. 4B).

e functional roles of these gene alterations were explored through GO and KEGG analyses, focusing on the top 100 genes with upregulated expression. Enrichment was observed in various biological processes, including pattern specification, DNA-binding transcriptional activator activity, and specific granule lumen (Fig. 4C). GSEA revealed significant enrichment of CTF1-related genes in immune response pathways such as NOD-like receptor signaling and antigen processing, along with tumorigenesis-related pathways such as Jak-Stat signaling and DNA methylation (Fig. 4D-O). Correlations between CTF1 expression and pathway scores related to tumor progression were assessed using GSVA and Spearman correlation analyses. Positive correlations were found between CTF1 expression and pathways involved in apoptosis, tumor inflammation, proliferation, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) signaling, and the PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway (Supplementary Fig. 3A-E). Collectively, these findings suggest a pivotal role for CTF1 in glioma development and modulation of immune responses, underlining its potential as a key player in tumor progression and immune regulation.

div.head: CTF1 expression in glioma is associated with immune infiltration
div.p: e aforementioned evidence suggests a potential link between CTF1 expression in glioma and tumor immunity. Subsequently, we examined the function of CTF1 in the immune microenvironment of glioma by analyzing data from TCGA. Analysis of Stromal scores, Immune scores, and ESTIMATE scores in glioma datasets revealed a positive correlation between CTF1 expression and immune infiltration within glioma specimens (Fig. 5A-C). Examination of the association between CTF1 expression and 24 immune cell types in glioma samples revealed significant positive correlations in most instances (Fig. 5D). Noteworthy variations in immune cell compositions were detected between the high and low CTF1 expression groups, with increased numbers of macrophages, eosinophils, and neutrophils in the high CTF1 expression group (Fig. 5E). GSEA highlighted positive links between high CTF1 expression and pathways such as T cell antigen receptor, PD1 signaling, and PD1 blocker cancer immunotherapy (Fig. 6A-C). Expression analysis revealed that the expression of key immune checkpoint-related genes, such as CDC274 and CTLA4, is upregulated in patients with high CTF1 expression, indicating a positive correlation between CTF1 and these genes (Fig. 6D-L). Moreover, single-cell transcriptome analysis using the TISCH database revealed CTF1 expression in various immune cell types in the glioma immune microenvironment (Supplementary Fig. 4A-C).
ese findings underscore the potential role of CTF1 in molding the immune landscape of glioma and signify its importance in modulating tumor immunity.

div.head: Reduced expression of CTF1 suppresses the proliferation and induces apoptosis of glioma cells in vitro
div.p: We investigated the role of CTF1 in glioma using siRNA knockdown methodology in U118MG and LN229 cell lines. RT-qPCR showed a significant reduction in CTF1 mRNA levels in the knockdown versus Fig. 3 Correlation between expression and DNA methylation and m6A RNA modification in glioma. A, B The visualization between the methylation level and the CTF1 expression. C-O The Kaplan-Meier survival of the promoter methylation of CTF1. C, D The distribution landscape of methylation probes. E Heatmap of the correlation between CTF1 and m6A-related genes in glioma. F The differential expression of m6A-related genes between high and low CTF1 expression groups in glioma samples. G, H Effects of m6A regulators on prognosis of glioma with different expression of CTF1. *P < 0.05. **P < 0.01. ***P < 0.001 (See figure on next page.) control groups, confirming successful knockdown (Supplementary Fig. 5A). Subsequently, a CCK8 assay was performed to evaluate cell proliferation after CTF1 knockdown. The findings indicated that the knockdown of CTF1 significantly inhibited the growth of U118MG and LN229 cell lines (Supplementary Fig. 5B). Concurrently, the clonogenic and sphereforming capacities of the tumor cells were inhibited (Supplementary Fig. 5C). Considering the previous GSEA results that suggested a correlation between CTF1-related genes and programmed cell death, and the positive correlation between CTF1 and apoptotic pathway score, we examined the effect of CTF1 on apoptosis as a potential mechanism to regulate glioma cell proliferation. Flow cytometry analysis indicated a significant increase in the apoptosis rates of U118MG and LN229 cells in the knockdown group compared to that in the control group (Supplementary Fig. 5D). These findings suggest that CTF1 may play a role in regulating the malignant progression of glioma cells.

div.head: Drug sensitivity analysis of CTF1
div.p: We explored the relationship between CTF1 expression and drug sensitivity using the CellMiner database to provide insights into associations with drug resistance in tumors. A significant negative correlation was observed between CTF1 levels and the sensitivity to 14 drugs, barring ofloxacin and TDP-665759 precursor intermediate in vitro (Supplementary Fig. 6). These results indicate that CTF1 could be a promising target for tumor drug therapy.

div.head: Discussion
div.p: Glioma, the most common malignant tumor of the central nervous system, has a high fatality rate despite its relatively low incidence. Glioblastoma, in particular, is the most common and aggressive form of malignant glioma, with a notoriously short survival time of less than 2 years [1,2]. Currently, the main treatment modalities for glioma include maximal tumor resection followed by adjuvant chemoradiotherapy. Despite these approaches, patient outcomes have not improved significantly. In recent years, electric field therapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy have shown promise in treating glioma, but owing to a lack of effective targets, patients with glioma do not experience clear benefits from various treatments [18]. Modern advancements in glioma molecular biology have identified important molecular markers such as IDH mutation, 1p/19q codeletion, O(6)-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) promoter methylation, and telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT) promoter mutation [19][20][21].

ese markers have contributed to the diagnosis, treatment, and prognosis of glioma, but they are insufficient to guide clinical decision-making and accurately predict overall survival in patients. erefore, it is imperative to explore new targets implicated in the onset and advancement of glioma, as these insights could significantly improve the diagnosis, therapeutic strategies, and prognosis of this condition. In this study, we used bioinformatics to examine the expression of CTF1 in glioma and assess its effects on patient prognosis. Our findings revealed an elevated CTF1 level in patients with glioma, which was often associated with adverse clinical and pathological characteristics. Additionally, our study identified CTF1 as a likely independent prognostic factor in glioma. By conducting knockdown experiments that targeted CTF1 on U118MG and LN229 glioma cell lines, we observed a decrease in glioma cell proliferation and clonogenicity, accompanied by an increase in apoptosis. Analysis of drug sensitivrevealed a strong inverse relationship between CTF1 expression and several anti-cancer agents, such as temsirolimus and vincristine.
ese findings indicate that CTF1 could be a promising therapeutic target for controlling glioma progression and a predictive marker for glioma patient prognosis.

e regulation of gene expression in human cells is an intricate and closely monitored process. Epigenetic changes serve as important controllers of different biological functions and are essential for cancer development and advancement. Among the various modifications, DNA methylation and m6A modification of mRNA are key types of epigenetic regulation [22][23][24]. Prior research has demonstrated a strong correlation between abnormal DNA methylation and tumor development. Dysregulated DNA methylation, whether through hypermethylation or hypomethylation, can interfere with gene expression patterns, ultimately promoting the initiation and progression of tumors [25][26][27]. Previous research has identified immune subtypes in patients with glioma by analyzing lncRNA methylation, revealing the relationship between DNA methylation, lncRNA, and immune regulation.

ese studies have highlighted the regulatory role of DNA methylation in lncRNA expression in glioblastoma immune-related subtypes [28]. Another study reported that the transcription factor SOX2 promotes stem-cell characteristics and tumor proliferation in glioblastoma cells by inhibiting TET2 and deactivating DNA modifications, specifically 5hmC and 5mC [29]. In our study, we observed elevated expression of CTF1 in glioma, concomitant with hypomethylation of the CTF1 promoter region. We hypothesize that hypomethylation of the promoter may promote cooperative interactions among distal regulatory elements, thereby facilitating the activation of gene expression mechanisms. Simultaneously, m6A modification, the most prevalent mRNA modification in eukaryotes, has demonstrated substantial involvement in tumorigenesis [30,31]. In glioblastoma, for example, BUD13 m6A methylation has been found to mediate angiogenic mimicry in glioblastoma cells [32]. Moreover, the m6A-mediated lncRNA WEE2-AS1 has been shown to promote glioblastoma progression by stabilizing RPN2 [33]. Additionally, the m6A-binding protein IGF2BP3 has been found to regulate the progression of renal clear cell carcinoma through the m6A-modified CDK4, mediated by DMDRMR [34]. Our examination of the TCGA database revealed a positive or negative correlations between CTF1 expression levels and the majority of m6A regulatory factors. We also found that the expression of the m6A writer WTAP and m6A readers IGF2BP2 and IGF2BP3 was upregulated in the high CTF1 expression group, potentially indicating an increased risk of malignant progression in gliomas.

is aligns with previous results suggesting that that dysregulated m6A writers and readers in gliomas often lead to malignant progression [35][36][37]. Furthermore, the comprehensive m6A regulatory network analysis demonstrated significant correlations between the expression of m6A regulatory factors in gliomas and patient prognosis. Research has indicated that the m6A reader YTHDF2 can influence hepatocellular carcinoma malignancy by regulating the mRNA levels of IL11, a member of the IL-6 family [38]. Based on these findings, we hypothesize that CTF1 expression is associated with m6A modifications in gliomas and regulated by factors such as WTAP, IGF2BP2, and IGF2BP3. In conclusion, the regulation of CTF1 expression in glioma may be influenced by DNA methylation and m6A modifications, thereby potentially affecting the malignant progression of this disease and adverse prognosis.

Our study identified a close link between CTF1 expression and biological processes pertinent to cell proliferation, such as DNA-binding transcription activator activity and RNA polymerase II specificity. Additionally, the GSVA results showed a positive correlation between CTF1 expression and scores of the tumor proliferation signaling, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, and apoptosis pathways. Experimental observations substantiated that elevated CTF1 levels promote glioma cell proliferation while simultaneously inhibiting apoptotic processes. Drawing on this data, we infer that CTF1 may expedite the onset and progression of glioma via its effect on glioma cell proliferation. Furthermore, our study elucidated connections between CTF1 and immune response-related pathways, including NOD-like receptor signaling, antigen processing, natural killer cell-mediated cytotoxicity, tolllike receptor signaling, and cell adhesion molecule signaling, among others. Abnormal immune infiltration in the tumor microenvironment is pivotal in promoting tumor cell proliferation, metastasis, and drug resistance [39], and previous gene functional enrichment analyses have revealed a tight association between CTF1 expression and numerous immune-related pathways. We focused on the effect of CTF1 on immune infiltration in the glioma microenvironment. Our observations indicated an increased presence of macrophages, eosinophils, and neutrophils in the high CTF1-expressing group. Previous studies have outlined similar phenomena, including circNEIL3-overexpressed glioma cells that promote malignancy via macrophage infiltration [40]. Additionally, eosinophils can impact tumor progression directly or indirectly [41]. Neutrophil infiltration levels correlate with resistance to immunotherapy and poor prognosis [42]. TISCH database analysis also indicated extensive CTF1 expression across microglia and mononuclear/ macrophage clusters. Additionally, a previous study has reported that in the early stages of renal cell carcinoma, IL-6 can induce macrophage infiltration and advance their polarization towards the tumor-promoting M2 phenotype, thereby facilitating the malignant progression of carcinoma [43]. A similar finding has been observed in colorectal cancer, where tumor-derived IL-6 promotes monocyte differentiation into tumor-supportive SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophages [44].

erefore, we speculate that CTF1 derived from glioma cells may promote glioma growth by inducing macrophage infiltration and polarization towards the M2 phenotype. In addition, Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) stimulate anti-tumor immune responses by disrupting T cell function [45][46][47][48], but the immunosuppressive nature of the central nervous system complicates their use in glioma treatment [49]. erefore, identifying potential glioma biomarkers that influence patient responses to ICI therapies is crucial [50]. Notably, our study established a strong positive relationship between CTF1 expression and the immune checkpoint-related genes CD274, PDCD1LG2, and HAVCR2, suggesting that CTF1 could potentially affects the response of patients with glioma to immunotherapy. ese findings propose a pivotal role for CTF1 in regulating the infiltration and functionality of immune cells in the glioma immune microenvironment.

is study has certain limitations and shortcomings. Firstly, to further validate CTF1 as a prognostic marker for glioma, it is essential to gather samples from multiple centers, which would enhance the generalizability of the findings. Secondly, while our investigation into the relationship between CTF1 and the glioma immune microenvironment primarily relied on bioinformatics approaches, further experimental studies are necessary to elucidate and confirm the role and molecular mechanisms by which CTF1 influences the immune landscape in gliomas. Additionally, more research is needed to explore the regulatory mechanisms affecting CTF1 expression and to assess its impact on the molecular pathways associated with the malignant phenotype of glioma. ese additional investigations will provide a more comprehensive understanding of CTF1's function and its potential as a therapeutic target.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this study, we performed an extensive bioinformatics analysis utilizing various databases and online tools to clarify the role of CTF1 in glioma. Our findings identify CTF1 as a significant independent prognostic factor that is closely associated with tumor immune microenvironment in glioma. Furthermore, we conducted in vitro phenotypic experiments to validate the functional relevance of CTF1. Notably, our results indicate that reduced CTF1 expression inhibits glioma cells proliferation while simultaneously triggering apoptosis. Collectively, CTF1 may be a promising prognostic biomarker and a target for the clinical treatment of glioma.
